title: Larval sablefish exhibit stable geographic distributions and variable phenology in response to interannually variable environmental conditions
content:
Abstract
Interannual variability in both local environmental conditions and basin-scale oceanographic modes of variability is thought to drive larval fish density by affecting the timing and location of spawning. We used an extensive compiled dataset of larval fish density from 1995 to 2018 from continental shelf regions off central California to the Gulf of Alaska (GOA) to model how sablefish (Anoplopoma fimbria) shifted larval seasonality and geography in response to environmental variability and oceanographic regime shifts. The most predictive spatiotemporal model was the simplest and did not include seasonal or geographic variability, with bottom depth and sea surface temperature as the most predictive environmental covariates. Sablefish larval distributions were centered in the shelf region of the eastern GOA and exhibited correlated shifts among latitudinal, longitudinal, and onshore–offshore center of gravities, but not with seasonal changes. There were few links between geographic and seasonal center of gravities and average environmental conditions, though modeled larval density peaked earlier in the year during warmer, spicier average ocean conditions and positive Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO) values. Phase-specific conditional effects models for the PDO and Oceanic Niño Index showed that sablefish larvae were uniformly associated with water temperatures between 7 and 8°C while having a more variable relationship with bottom depth. Our results indicate that sablefish larvae demonstrate seasonal shifts in order to maintain a consistent thermal habitat.
